introduction: These readings say, in every key, that the visible world passes: possessions change hands overnight, kings and palaces are dust, a life is a few brief days, and nothing endures but what is done for God. They draw from this detachment, justice in the use of power and wealth, service while there is time, and consolation in grief; some go further and call the world worthless. A hundred of the guide's three hundred quotations are read here, in the proportions of its seven sections, beside a hundred from elsewhere. Most stand alongside, for few themes are more widely shared: the Preacher, the psalms, Job, the Gospels, the Qur'an, Khayyam, Shakespeare, Gray, Shelley, Marcus Aurelius. Twelve push back or add a side: Genesis and the Wisdom of Solomon say that God made the world good and loves it, Nietzsche begs us to stay true to the earth, Keats and Hopkins find joy and praise in passing things, Herrick and Macbeth draw other conclusions from the same brevity, and Candide tends a garden.
questions: The readings say that tonight your possessions are yours and tomorrow another's. What changes in how you hold something once you believe that?
Genesis calls the world very good, and the Wisdom of Solomon says that God loves all that He has made. Some readings call the world worthless. In what sense can both be said?
Herrick, Macbeth and these readings all start from the shortness of life and end in different places. What makes the difference?
The readings turn transience into a reason to serve while there is time. What would you do this year if you took that seriously?
To someone newly bereaved, which of these passages console, and which would you not say? Why?
Nietzsche says: remain true to the earth. What do the readings keep faith with, and is the earth included?

outside.why: In the parable God says to the man with full barns: this night thy soul shall be required of thee; then whose shall those things be?
Jesus says: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal.
Paul's letter says that we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.
The psalm says that man's days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth, and the wind passeth over it.
Heraclitus said that you cannot step twice into the same rivers, for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
Lamentations begins: how doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!
Jesus says that no man can serve two masters: ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Proverbs says: keep thy heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life.
The psalm says: put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
Genesis says that God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. How can a world be of no worth in God's sight and also be what he looked on and called very good?
Paul tells his readers to use this world as not abusing it, for the fashion of this world passeth away.
The Preacher concludes his book on vanity: fear God, and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.
Jesus tells of a merchant who, finding one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Shakespeare's Prospero says that the cloud-capped towers, the gorgeous palaces and the great globe itself shall dissolve, and leave not a rack behind.
Shakespeare's Richard says that within the hollow crown of a king Death keeps his court, and comes at the last with a little pin.
The Preacher says: vanity of vanities, all is vanity; what profit hath a man of all his labour under the sun?
James asks whence come wars and fightings, and answers: of your lusts; ye desire to have, and cannot obtain.
Job says: naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither.
Khayyam, in FitzGerald's version, says that the lion and the lizard keep the courts where Jamshyd gloried and drank deep.
Jesus tells of a rich man clothed in purple who fared sumptuously every day, and of the beggar laid at his gate.
Shelley's traveller finds the words 'Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' on a pedestal, and nothing beside remains.
Jesus asks what it shall profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul.
Voltaire's Candide, after every calamity and every argument, concludes only that we must take care of our garden. If the conflicts of the world are a mirage, what is still worth doing in it?
Daniel reads the writing on the wall to a feasting king: God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.
The psalm says that man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.
Isaiah addresses a fallen king: how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!
Jesus, on trial for his life, says to the governor: my kingdom is not of this world.
Kipling wrote at the height of empire that all our pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
Gray writes in a country churchyard that the boast of heraldry and the pomp of power await alike the inevitable hour.
James says to those who plan a year of buying and selling: what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time.
Proverbs says that riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven.
The Preacher says that one generation passeth away, and another generation cometh, but the earth abideth for ever.
Jesus says that a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Jesus says that the tree is known by his fruit, and tells his hearers to make the tree good.
The psalm asks: so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Marcus Aurelius meets each morning with the thought that he is rising to the work of a human being.
Paul says that he counts all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ.
Genesis says: in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground, for out of it wast thou taken.
Jesus says: I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day; the night cometh, when no man can work.
The letter to the Hebrews says: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.

Herrick starts from the same fact, that this same flower that smiles today tomorrow will be dying, and concludes: gather ye rosebuds while ye may. Why do the same few brief days lead him to pleasure and this reading to service?
Paul writes: let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
The psalm says that the earth is full of the goodness of the Lord. Is that the same earth whose whole dominion is said here to be worth less than the wing of a gnat?
Jesus speaks of eighteen on whom a tower fell, and turns the news into a call to his hearers to change.
John's letter says that the world passeth away, and the lust thereof, but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
Shakespeare's Macbeth also calls life a walking shadow, a brief candle, and concludes that it signifies nothing. What makes the same shadow, in this reading, a time for joy and gladness?
The Preacher says that all go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Isaiah says that the grass withereth and the flower fadeth, but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately, so as not to discover, when he came to die, that he had not lived.
Job says that his days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and that his life is wind.
Wordsworth calls little, nameless, unremembered acts of kindness and of love the best portion of a good man's life.
Longfellow's psalm of life says: trust no future, let the dead past bury its dead; act in the living present.
Peter's letter says that the elements shall melt with fervent heat, and the earth and the works therein shall be burned up.
The psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
This is the verse quoted, in another place of the Qur'an: everything will perish save His countenance.
Keats begins a poem: a thing of beauty is a joy for ever; it will never pass into nothingness. Is there anything in the visible world that these readings would allow to be such a joy?
Thoreau observed that the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation, and that what is called resignation is confirmed desperation.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote that earth's crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God, but only he who sees takes off his shoes. Is a song that gladdens its hearers part of the fleeting world or a sight of something through it?
King David, when his child had died, said: I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.
Malachi has God say: I am the Lord, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Plato pictures prisoners in a den who take for real the shadows thrown on the wall before them by a fire behind.
Jesus says: take therefore no thought for the morrow; sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
Kipling asks whether you can meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same.
Hannah sings that the Lord bringeth low and lifteth up, and raiseth up the poor out of the dust.
The psalm has a refrain for what does not pass: give thanks unto the Lord, for his mercy endureth for ever.
Paul writes that he knows both how to be abased and how to abound, and has learned to be content.
Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita to be equable in good or evil, for equability is piety.
The Preacher says that to every thing there is a season: a time to weep, and a time to laugh.
Augustine prays: you have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.
Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise in heart mourn not for those that live, nor those that die.
Shakespeare's Jaques says that all the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players, with their exits and their entrances.
David laments over Saul and Jonathan: how are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle!
Tennyson, mourning his friend, holds it true that it is better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all. If every union here ends in separation, is the union the less worth having?
Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle.
Habakkuk says that though the fig tree shall not blossom and the fields yield no meat, yet he will rejoice in the Lord.
Hopkins tells a child grieving over falling leaves that sorrow's springs are the same: it is the blight man was born for.
John sees a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away.
The Preacher says that two are better than one, for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.
The letter to the Hebrews says that whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and tells its readers not to faint.

Nietzsche's Zarathustra begs his hearers to remain true to the earth, and not to believe those who speak of superearthly hopes. What would he call ignorance: being bound to this world, or being weaned from it?
Mary sings that God hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree.
The psalm says that weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
Paul cries out: O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
Marcus Aurelius tells himself to be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, and which stands firm.
The Preacher says that as the beast dieth, so dieth the man, and that all is vanity.
The psalmist says that he has quieted himself, as a child that is weaned of his mother.
Paul says that the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
The psalmist asks to know the measure of his days, which are as an handbreadth, and how frail he is.
The Qur'an says that the life of the world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry, and rivalry in wealth and children.
Paul says that three things abide, faith, hope and charity, and that the greatest of these is charity.
Hopkins gives glory to God for dappled things, whatever is fickle, freckled, swift or slow, and says that he who fathers them forth is past change. Can the fading of mortal charm itself be praised?
The Dhammapada says that not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea, nor in the clefts of the mountains is there a spot where death could not overcome us.
Mill held that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied, better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
Paul writes that it is high time to awake out of sleep: the night is far spent, the day is at hand.
The psalmist says that a day in the courts of the Lord is better than a thousand elsewhere.
The Song of Solomon says that many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.
The psalm says that the heavens shall wax old like a garment and be changed, but thou art the same.

Paul's letter says that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. Is it unseemly to set one's affections on what is good, or only to set them there last?
Thoreau called our inventions pretty toys which distract our attention from serious things: improved means to an unimproved end.

The Wisdom of Solomon says to God: thou lovest all the things that are, and abhorrest nothing which thou hast made. If God loves the world of dust, what is the right sense in which a soul may grow contemptuous of it?
